claims.text: Met acidosis: tx the cause; hemodialysis for renal failure and sometimes for ethylene glycol, methanol or salicylate poisoning
claims.quote: Treatment is directed at the cause. Hemodialysis is required for renal failure and sometimes for ethylene glycol, methanol, or salicylate poisoning.

claims.text: Bicarb by AG: generally safe and appropriate in norm AG acidosis (HCO3 loss or inorganic acids); controversial in ↑AG acidosis (organic acids), where it does ⍉clearly lower mortality
claims.quote: When metabolic acidosis results from loss of HCO3− or accumulation of inorganic acids (ie, normal anion gap acidosis), bicarbonate therapy is generally safe and appropriate. However, when acidosis results from organic acid accumulation (ie, high anion gap acidosis), bicarbonate therapy is controversial; it does not clearly decrease mortality in these conditions, and there are several possible risks.

claims.text: Bicarb risks: overshoot met alkalosis once lactate and ketoacids are met, sodium and vol overload, hypokalemia, and hypercapnia
claims.quote: With treatment of the underlying condition, lactate and ketoacids are metabolized back to HCO3−; exogenous HCO3− loading may therefore cause an “overshoot” metabolic alkalosis. In any condition, giving sodium bicarbonate may also cause sodium and volume overload, hypokalemia, and, by inhibiting respiratory drive, hypercapnia.

claims.text: Severe met acidosis (pH < 7.0): most experts give IV bicarb, ← worsening cardiovasc instability @ lower pH
claims.quote: Despite these and other controversies, most experts recommend giving bicarbonate IV for severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.0) primarily because of concerns about worsening cardiovascular instability at lower pH values.

claims.text: Bicarb target: raise HCO3 only to the level that gives a pH of 7.10, ie, desired HCO3 = 0.30 × PCO2
claims.quote: The first is the level to which HCO3− must be raised, calculated by the Kassirer-Bleich equation, using a target value for [H+] of 79 nEq/L (79 nmol/L), which corresponds to a pH of 7.10: [H+] = 79 = 24 × Pco2/HCO3− or Desired HCO3−= 0.30 × Pco2

claims.text: Bicarb dose: NaHCO3 (mEq) = (desired HCO3 − observed HCO3) × 0.4 × body wt (kg)
claims.quote: The amount of sodium bicarbonate needed to achieve that level is NaHCO3 required (mEq/mmol) = (desired [HCO3−] − observed [HCO3−]) × 0.4 × body weight (kg)

claims.text: Giving it: over several hrs; recheck blood pH and HCO3 30 minutes to 1 hr afterward
claims.quote: This amount of sodium bicarbonate is given over several hours. Blood pH and HCO3− levels can be checked 30 minutes to 1 hour after administration, which allows for equilibration with extravascular HCO3−.

claims.text: Ampules: a typical 50-mL ampule holds 50 mEq; several given quickly can worsen vol overload and cause hyperosmolality
claims.quote: it is important to realize that the typical 50-mL ampule of NaHCO3 contain 50 mEq of sodium bicarbonate and can worsen volume overload and also cause hyperosmolality especially if multiple ampules are given over a short period time.

claims.text: Watch potassium: K depletion = common in met acidosis; monitor serum K often and replace w oral or IV KCl
claims.quote: Potassium (K+) depletion, common in metabolic acidosis, should be identified through frequent serum K+ monitoring and treated as needed with oral or parenteral potassium chloride.

claims.text: Met alkalosis: tx the underlying condition, paying particular attention to correcting hypovolemia and hypokalemia
claims.quote: Underlying conditions are treated, with particular attention paid to correction of hypovolemia and hypokalemia.

claims.text: Which kind: urine Cl < 20 mEq/L points to a chloride-responsive cause; > 20 mEq/L suggests a chloride-unresponsive form
claims.quote: Urinary Cl < 20 mEq/L (< 20 mmol/L) indicates significant renal Cl− reabsorption and hence a Cl-responsive cause (see table Causes of Metabolic Alkalosis) Urinary Cl > 20 mEq/L (> 20 mmol/L) suggests a chloride-unresponsive form.

claims.text: Chloride-responsive: 0.9% saline IV, typically 50 to 100 mL/hr more than urinary and other fluid losses, until urine Cl rises to > 25 mEq/L
claims.quote: Patients with chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis are given 0.9% saline solution IV; infusion rate is typically 50 to 100 mL/hour greater than urinary and other sensible and insensible fluid losses until urinary Cl rises to > 25 mEq/L (> 25 mmol/L) and urinary pH normalizes after an initial rise from bicarbonaturia.

claims.text: Chloride-unresponsive: rehydration alone rarely helps; tx the specific cause; potassium and magnesium supplements and/or potassium-sparing diuretics are USU needed
claims.quote: Patients with chloride-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis rarely benefit from rehydration alone and requires treating the specific cause. Potassium and magnesium supplementation and/or potassium-sparing diuretics are usually needed.

claims.text: Severe met alkalosis (ex, pH > 7.6): hemofiltration or hemodialysis = an option, esp w vol overload and renal dysfun; acetazolamide 250 to 375 mg once or twice a day increases HCO3 excretion but can also increase K and phosphate losses
claims.quote: Patients with severe metabolic alkalosis (eg, pH > 7.6) sometimes require more urgent correction of blood pH. Hemofiltration or hemodialysis is an option, particularly if volume overload and renal dysfunction are present. Acetazolamide 250 to 375 mg orally or IV once or twice a day increases HCO3− excretion but may also accelerate urinary losses of K+ and phosphate (PO4−); volume-overloaded patients with diuretic-induced metabolic alkalosis and those with posthypercapnic metabolic alkalosis may especially benefit.

claims.text: Resp acidosis: adequate ventilation, by endotracheal intubation or noninvasive (+) P ventilation, = all that = needed
claims.quote: Treatment is provision of adequate ventilation by either endotracheal intubation or noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (for specific indications and procedures, see Overview of Respiratory Failure). Adequate ventilation is all that is needed to correct respiratory acidosis.

claims.text: Chronic hypercapnia: lower PCO2 slowly (over several hrs or more); lowering it too fast → a posthypercapnic overshoot alkalosis that can lead to seizures and death
claims.quote: Chronic hypercapnia generally must be corrected slowly (eg, over several hours or more) because too-rapid Pco2 lowering can cause a posthypercapnic “overshoot” alkalosis when the underlying compensatory hyperbicarbonatemia becomes unmasked. The abrupt rise in CNS pH that results can lead to seizures and death.

claims.text: Also: correct any potassium and Cl deficits
claims.quote: Any potassium and chloride deficits are corrected.

claims.text: Bicarb in resp acidosis: almost always contraindicated, ← poss paradoxical CNS acidosis
claims.quote: Sodium bicarbonate is almost always contraindicated because of the potential for paradoxical acidosis within the CNS.
